title: The Prince
author: Niccolò Machiavelli
openingText: Those who wish to win a prince's favor customarily come before him with whatever they hold most precious, or whatever they see him take most delight in. So one often sees princes presented with horses, arms, cloth of gold, precious stones, and similar ornaments worthy of their greatness.
about:
The Prince asks how rulers acquire power, keep it, and lose it. Its twenty-six chapters move from types of principality to armies, advisers, reputation, cruelty, promises, and fortune. Machiavelli tests his advice against examples from ancient history and the Italian politics of his own time. The closing chapter calls on the Medici family to lead Italy's liberation from foreign domination.

The argument often turns on distinctions: inherited power versus newly acquired power, one's own soldiers versus hired or borrowed forces, fear versus hatred, and a reputation for goodness versus the consequences of good conduct. Machiavelli's praise of particular actions is part of his argument, not a guarantee that his historical explanations are complete. His language also carries the prejudices and violence of its period.

This edition follows W. K. Marriott's English translation. The modern English and Danish preserve its chapters and paragraph structure, including the older translator's notes. Identified factual errors in those notes are explicitly corrected; a small number of reversed or unclear readings are clarified against the Italian. Modernized verse is identified as a rendering rather than an exact quotation. In this book, virtù often means ability, resolve, or effective action rather than moral virtue; fortune means the changing circumstances a ruler cannot fully control.

angleCards.title: Power and its foundations
angleCards.text: Follow the distinction between acquiring a state and keeping it. When does outside help create dependence, and when can a new ruler build support of his own?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to trace how The Prince distinguishes gaining power from keeping it, especially through armies, allies, and popular support.

angleCards.title: Fear, hatred, and harm
angleCards.text: Read the qualifications around the famous preference for being feared. Compare the arguments about punishment, property, military discipline, and avoiding hatred.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine Machiavelli's arguments about fear and cruelty, including their qualifications and the costs his examples leave out.

angleCards.title: Skill and fortune
angleCards.text: Compare the ruler who prepares for a flood with the ruler whose habits no longer fit the times. How much freedom does the book allow, and how consistent is its advice?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand the relationship between personal ability and fortune, and test the tension between adapting to circumstances and acting decisively.

cast.name: Niccolò Machiavelli
cast.description: Addresses Lorenzo de' Medici in the dedication and presents knowledge of rulers' actions as his gift. His method compares historical examples and asks what helps a prince retain power.

cast.name: Cesare Borgia
cast.role: A new ruler's rise and fall
cast.description: The central example in chapter 7. Machiavelli follows his dependence on his father's power and foreign troops, his efforts to build his own position, and the collapse that followed.

cast.name: Julius II
cast.description: A pope whose rapid, forceful actions serve as an example of a temperament suited to its moment. Machiavelli asks what would happen if circumstances instead demanded caution.

cast.name: Hannibal and Scipio
cast.description: In chapter 17, Machiavelli contrasts Hannibal's harsh discipline with Scipio's leniency to explore the relationship between military authority, cruelty, and obedience.

cast.name: The new prince
cast.description: A ruler who must establish authority rather than rely on inheritance. His problems connect the chapters on conquest, armies, supporters, advisers, and reputation.

cast.name: Fortune
cast.description: Personified as a force that resists control. The flood metaphor stresses preparation; the later violent gendered metaphor stresses boldness. Both belong to Machiavelli's historical argument.

whyItMatters.title: Arguments behind familiar sayings
whyItMatters.body: The chapters on love and fear, promises, and appearances are easier to assess when read with their surrounding qualifications. The book repeatedly distinguishes effective power from moral reputation.

whyItMatters.title: Examples that can be questioned
whyItMatters.body: The historical cases are not decorative. They carry the reasoning. Ask whether each example supports the proposed rule, and whether the same events could support another explanation.

whyItMatters.title: Advice under pressure
whyItMatters.body: The book weighs choices that cannot all be made safe. Its claims about necessity invite close scrutiny: who decides what is necessary, who bears the harm, and what counts as success?
